clue.text: High, as mature hams

indicators.note: someone high is intoxicated and muddled, so the following letters come out in a confused order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Two ageing actors, apparently a little tipsy, hamming it up on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' reads as a description of the hams but is the signal to rearrange 'as mature' into AMATEURS.
explanation.definitionFit: A ham is an unskilled performer or a hobbyist radio operator, so hams are people doing things without professional status.

clue.text: Request loudly a spa treatment

indicators.note: something said loudly is spoken out, so we go by how the words sound rather than how they are spelt

blocks.note: a peel is a skin treatment offered at a spa, here with the article 'a' in front

explanation.surface: Someone asking, rather too loudly, to be booked in for a beauty treatment at a spa.
explanation.definitionFit: To make an earnest plea or petition for something is the verb sense matching asking for it.

clue.text: Tennis champ's a lot of fun in Spain, I agree

blocks.note: taken as written
a gas is informal for a great deal of fun
si is Spanish for yes

explanation.surface: A tennis star on holiday in Spain is having a whale of a time, and the speaker concurs.
explanation.walkthrough: Andre Agassi won eight Grand Slam singles titles.
explanation.definitionFit: Andre Agassi is a former world number one player, so he is an example of a champion of the sport.

clue.text: Perhaps Magritte, creator of unsettling images, the old revolutionary, produces revelation

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the whole string of pieces is read the other way

blocks.note: Magritte's first name was René; 'perhaps' because other people share it
Edgar Allan Poe wrote unsettling, macabre tales
ye is an archaic form of the

explanation.surface: An art critic praising Magritte, the surrealist painter of disturbing pictures, as a radical whose work enlightens.
explanation.walkthrough: Magritte looks like the subject, but only his first name is used; Poe, not Magritte, is the creator of unsettling images. RENE POE YE read backwards gives EYE-OPENER.
explanation.definitionFit: Something surprising that shows you a truth you had not seen is a startling disclosure, a sudden enlightening discovery.

clue.text: Fruit salad ingredient? That's not technically a fruit etc etc

blocks.clueFragment: Fruit salad ingredient? That's not technically a fruit
blocks.note: surface reading: a plant stalk cooked like a fruit in desserts, though botanically it is a vegetable
setter's reading: the meaningless murmur actors repeat to suggest background conversation, doubled as 'etc' is doubled

explanation.surface: A pedant interrupts a recipe to point out that one ingredient of the fruit salad is really a vegetable, and so on.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhubarb is botanically a vegetable; 'rhubarb rhubarb' is what extras mutter on stage to sound like a crowd, so the word appears twice just as 'etc' does.
explanation.definitionFit: Meaningless background chatter or nonsense is the idiomatic sense, a filler phrase standing in for unspecified talk like 'and so on'.

clue.text: Working with American on island, heading west

indicators.note: in an across answer, heading west means travelling right to left, so the island is written backwards

blocks.note: US is short for American
Elba is the Mediterranean island of Napoleon's exile

explanation.surface: An American working holiday on an island, travelling westwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in working order is fit to be put into service, functional and serviceable.

clue.text: Expensive taste epicure has

indicators.note: the phrase is said to have the answer inside it, holding it within its letters

blocks.note: running across the two words

explanation.surface: A gourmet has refined, costly preferences in food.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep price is an informal way of saying a charge is too high, so costly.

clue.text: Gall bladder – boo! – removed without hesitation

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letters for the hesitation are taken out
removed in the sense of moved about, displaced from their original order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
er is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: A surgeon swiftly takes out a gall bladder while someone jeers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gall bladder' reads as a single organ, but gall alone is the definition and the organ's name is raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Gall is bitterness or rancour, and bad blood is the idiom for lasting ill feeling or resentment between people.

clue.text: Examines cocktails in the Queen Vic

indicators.note: the Queen Vic is the East London pub in the soap EastEnders, so the word is pronounced in a Cockney accent that drops the h

blocks.note: highballs are long cocktails; with the h dropped they are said 'ighballs

explanation.surface: Someone inspects the drinks served at a famous soap-opera pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen Vic is the pub in EastEnders, a BBC soap set in Cockney London, where the h of highballs would be dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball something is informal for looking it over closely, staring at or inspecting it.

clue.text: Cruddy actor was cast as Chicken

indicators.note: cast as in thrown or moulded anew, so the letters are reshaped into a different order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A dreadful actor was given the part of a chicken in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast as' sounds like theatre casting; 'cast' alone is the anagram signal and 'as' joins it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicken is slang for a timid person, and this childish taunt names someone who is easily frightened.

clue.text: Level up late, audacious to some extent

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, a stretch of its letters rather than all of them

blocks.note: running across the three words

explanation.surface: A gamer stays up late and boldly reaches the next level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Level up' is a gaming phrase, but 'Level' alone is the definition and 'up' starts the hidden letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plateau is a flat stretch of high ground, and also a stage where progress stays flat.

clue.text: Unsettled, startled, devoured abruptly

indicators.note: abruptly means cut off suddenly, so the word loses its final letter
a startled thing jumps and is jolted out of place, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written before its end is cut

explanation.surface: A frightened, jumpy creature gulps its food down in a hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: An unsettled bill or debt is one not yet paid, so its payment is late beyond the due date.

clue.text: On 2nd of March, sit back for storyteller

indicators.note: the second of a word means just its second letter is kept
going back means reading from the end towards the start

blocks.note: the second letter of March
to sit for a portrait is to pose

explanation.surface: On the second of March, someone sits down again to hear a tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek author credited with the fables, a teller of moral animal tales.

clue.text: A better piano? Fitzgerald is unaccompanied

blocks.note: taken as written
to cap something is to better or outdo it
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
Ella Fitzgerald, the jazz singer

explanation.surface: A jazz fan asks whether a better pianist could be found, since Ella Fitzgerald is singing alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like an adjective describing the piano, but it is the verb cap.
explanation.definitionFit: Singing a cappella means performing with voices alone, without instrumental backing.

clue.text: Failure for starter, summer pudding: one's not swallowed much

indicators.note: a starter is what comes first, so only the opening letter of the next word is kept

blocks.note: a nobody is a person who has failed to make a mark
the first letter of summer
a fool is a British dessert of puréed fruit folded into cream

explanation.surface: A disappointing meal: a poor first course and a summer pudding of which hardly anyone ate much.
explanation.walkthrough: The menu words starter and pudding misdirect; 'swallowed' means believed, as in swallowing a lie.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is nobody's fool is shrewd and cannot be duped, a person who does not swallow tall stories.

clue.text: Horribly evil friar's removed a tree

indicators.note: removed means taken away, so one letter comes out of the collection
something done horribly is badly messed up, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe ignored
the letter to be taken out

explanation.surface: A wicked monk has cut down a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: One A comes out of EVIL FRIARS and the nine letters left are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The silver fir is a European conifer with silvery undersides to its needles, a kind of tree.

clue.text: A little insect eaten by son

indicators.note: whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a midge is a tiny biting fly

explanation.surface: A boy has accidentally swallowed a tiny bug.
explanation.definitionFit: A smidgeon is a very small amount, a tiny bit or trace of something.

clue.text: Everyman is grabbing ten and dancing together

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and swap places before settling
grabbing means holding hold of, so the outer piece clutches the other inside it

blocks.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I, and 'is' becomes 'm
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The puzzle's setter takes ten partners and they all dance together.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming themself in a clue usually means I or ME; here 'Everyman is' is I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Working in tandem means acting jointly or side by side, cooperating as one unit.

clue.text: Manic choral arrangement befitting royals

indicators.note: an arrangement sets things in a new order, as with a musical piece rescored

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A frenzied choir piece arranged for a royal occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arrangement' fits the musical surface but signals rearranging the letters of 'Manic choral'.
explanation.definitionFit: Monarchical describes things relating to a king or queen, so suitable for a sovereign and court.

clue.text: Searches for weapons

blocks.note: first meaning: rummages through hastily, as a burglar does a drawer
second meaning: long-barrelled guns fired from the shoulder

explanation.surface: Police comb an area looking for firearms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Searches for' reads as one phrase, but 'for' merely links the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for ransacking through belongings and a plural noun for long guns.

clue.text: Primarily, something your zodiac's 'yoking' gives you?

definitions.text: Primarily, something your zodiac's 'yoking' gives you?

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so the opening letter of each following word is kept

blocks.note: the initial letters of the six words

explanation.surface: An astrologer asks what the alignment in your star sign brings you.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the initials spell the word, and the clue describes it as a yoking found in astrology.
explanation.definitionFit: Syzygy is the alignment of three celestial bodies, from a Greek word meaning yoked together.

clue.text: Races after admiral, oddly wanting to make speeches

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the odd-numbered letters go and only the even ones remain

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of admiral
a race or people can be called a tribe

explanation.surface: Peoples follow a strange naval commander who wishes to address them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the races second, behind the admiral letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A diatribe is a bitter, forceful verbal attack, a ranting speech or tirade.

clue.text: Regularly defective drier's best turned off and on again

indicators.note: defective at regular intervals means every other letter is missing, leaving alternate ones

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A tumble dryer keeps breaking down, and the best fix is to switch it off and on.
explanation.walkthrough: The IT helpdesk cure suits the surface; the definition is a participle, matching the answer's past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: A device that has been reset has been restarted, put back to its starting state after switching off.

clue.text: A Brontë vacuously missing the point

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so the following letters are dropped from the word

blocks.note: acting vacuously is acting emptily
pt is a standard abbreviation for point

explanation.surface: A novelist from the famous literary family comes across as mindless, failing to grasp what matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing the point' sounds like a criticism of the novelist; the letters P and T are removed from the middle of the adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily Brontë wrote Wuthering Heights and was one of the three famous writing sisters.

clue.text: Customer spluttering 'Rudeness!' cut short

indicators.note: cut short means the word is trimmed at its end, losing the final letter
spluttering speech comes out garbled and broken, so the letters emerge disordered

blocks.note: taken as written before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: A shopper splutters indignantly at an insult before being interrupted.
explanation.definitionFit: The end user is the person who finally uses a product, the consumer or client buying it.

clue.text: Horribly legally decapitated

indicators.note: decapitated means beheaded, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: acting legally is acting lawfully

explanation.surface: A grim report of a gruesome but judicially sanctioned beheading.
explanation.definitionFit: Awfully means in a dreadful or terrible way, very badly indeed.

clue.text: Greek character, politician, heartless tiny fool

indicators.note: without its heart the word keeps only its outside letters

blocks.note: nu is a letter of the Greek alphabet
MP is a Member of Parliament
the first and last letters of tiny

explanation.surface: A cruel Greek politician is dismissed as a small-minded idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: Numpty is Scottish slang for an idiot, now used throughout Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A numpty is an informal British word for a stupid or inept person, an idiot.

clue.text: It's likely that Ray's idea is kinky

indicators.note: kinky means twisted or bent, so these letters are bent into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone suspects that Ray's proposal is rather risqué.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying I dare say means you think something probable, accepting it as quite possibly true.
